analysis.one_liner: Would suspend the post-crisis ban on banks trading for their own profit until foreign rivals face matching rules.
analysis.headline: Introduced with three cosponsors and referred to committee the same day, the bill died there without a hearing, markup, or vote when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law bars banks that hold federally insured deposits from trading securities for their own profit and from owning hedge funds — the "Volcker Rule," written after the 2008 crisis. This bill would suspend those bans until the Treasury Secretary certified that nine foreign countries impose equivalent restrictions on their own banks. Banks could demand hearings and sue over any certification, and the bans would stay suspended while that played out. Because none of those countries has such a ban, the rule would in practice stay shelved indefinitely.
analysis.who_benefits: Big banks with large trading operations. They would keep betting their own capital on markets while customer deposits remain federally insured, and they could resume owning and sponsoring hedge funds and private equity funds. The bill is built to let them make that case to Treasury, in hearings, and in court for as long as it takes.

how_it_helps.text: Suspends the ban on banks trading for their own accounts and owning or sponsoring hedge funds and private equity funds until the Treasury Secretary certifies that competing foreign countries impose equivalent restrictions.

Directs Treasury to identify banks in nine named countries — the UK, France, Germany, Switzerland, Japan, Brazil, China, Canada, and Mexico — that compete significantly with U.S. banks, and to certify each country's rules as equivalent.
Gives banks and other interested parties a formal hearing and the right to sue over any certification in federal appeals court, and keeps the trading bans postponed while that review is pending.

analysis.who_pays: The public. The trading ban exists to keep speculation losses at banks from landing on insured depositors and taxpayers, as happened in the 2008 crisis; shelving it shifts that risk back onto a system everyone else pays to rescue.

drawbacks.text: The bill answers a real complaint: U.S. banks argued they would lose trading business to foreign rivals not bound by the rule, and the bill's entire design — conditioning the ban on certified foreign equivalence — is built around that concern.

The equivalence bar was almost certainly unreachable, since none of the nine named countries imposed a proprietary-trading ban, so the bill would not have delayed the rule so much as ended it by another name — an honest supporter would have to concede that.
Even a temporary delay carries cost: banks' own speculative trades would stay funded by insured deposits, the risk the rule was written to end after the 2008 crisis.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If foreign banks were about to face equivalent rules, the bill would be a defensible way to protect U.S. banks' competitiveness. They were not: the certification standard, the hearings, and the court review built into the bill made indefinite suspension the realistic outcome. The honest weighing is that the bill offered the public continued protection on paper while arranging for that protection to never actually bind, and it died before that trade could be made.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee in December 2013, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter King (R-NY) introduced the bill on Dec. 11, 2013, with Reps. Huizenga (R-MI), Grimm (R-NY), and Miller (R-CA) as original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day.
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — and the bill died when the 113th Congress ended on Jan. 3, 2015.
The trading bans carried their own effective date under existing law — the earlier of 12 months after final rules were issued or two years after enactment — so they proceeded without this bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary depositors and taxpayers: the restriction on banks trading with insured deposits stayed on track, and the banks seeking the delay got nothing for their effort.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Depositors and taxpayers kept the safeguard

for.name: Rep. Peter T. King
for.role: U.S. Representative from New York; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to delay the Volcker Rule's trading bans until foreign banks face equivalent restrictions.

for.name: Reps. Bill Huizenga, Michael Grimm, and Gary G. Miller
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill on the day it was introduced.

for.name: U.S. banking industry
for.role: Banks and trade groups pressing on the Volcker Rule
for.what_they_did: Ran a well-publicized campaign to delay and soften the Volcker Rule's trading ban — the outcome this bill would have written into law.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral — chaired by Rep. Jeb Hensarling (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill's referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — and the bill died there when the 113th Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All four members who put the bill forward were Republicans, but it never reached a vote and the Republican-led committee that held it took no recorded action, so no roll call shows where anyone else stood.

industries.industry: Large banks with proprietary trading desks
industries.note: The bill would let banks resume trading for their own profit and sponsoring hedge funds while their deposits stay federally insured — profits to the bank, losses backstopped by the public. That is the exact arrangement the Volcker Rule was written to end.

industries.industry: Hedge funds and private equity funds
industries.note: Banks could again own and sponsor these funds, restoring a large channel of bank capital into them. The public risk runs through the banks' balance sheets rather than the funds themselves.
